title: Visual Propaganda Through History
objective: Students will analyze how visual manipulation has been used to influence public opinion throughout history, identify six common propaganda techniques, and apply critical analysis skills to both historical and contemporary examples.
materials: WWI/WWII recruitment and propaganda posters (multiple nations)
Soviet-era doctored photographs (showing removed political figures)
Modern examples of political image manipulation (age-appropriate)
connection: **Option 1 — Visit:** Spirit photography examples show how visual manipulation exploited grief for profit. Victorian illusion cards demonstrate the era’s fascination with visual trickery.

steps.title: The Disappearing Commissar
script: Display two versions of the famous Soviet photograph — the original showing Stalin with Nikolai Yezhov at the Moscow Canal, and the altered version with Yezhov removed after his 1940 execution.
“These are the same photograph, taken on the same day. What’s different?”
Let students identify the missing person.

screen.question: These are the same photograph, taken on the same day. What’s different?

steps.purpose: Students spot the erased man before they hear why he was erased.

steps.title: Erased from photographs
script: “In the Soviet Union under Stalin, when political leaders fell out of favor — often executed — they were literally erased from photographs. The government controlled what people could see, rewriting history by manipulating images.”

screen.question: The government controlled what people could see, rewriting history by manipulating images.

steps.purpose: Name what the erasure was for: control of what people could see.
students: Why erase someone from a photograph?

steps.title: Define propaganda
script: **Define propaganda:** Information — especially biased or misleading — used to promote a political cause. Not always lies; often selective truth, emotional manipulation, or exaggeration.

screen.question: Information — especially biased or misleading — used to promote a political cause.

steps.purpose: A working definition to test every example against.
students: Not always lies; often selective truth, emotional manipulation, or exaggeration.

steps.title: Six Propaganda Techniques
script: **Bandwagon:** “Everyone is doing it — join in!” Appeals to desire to belong.
**Fear:** “Something terrible will happen if you don’t act.” Appeals to survival.
**Name-Calling:** Negative labels to create prejudice. Depicts enemies as subhuman.
**Glittering Generalities:** Vague positive words: “Freedom,” “Honor,” “Patriotism.”
**Transfer:** Connecting respected symbols (flag, family) to your cause.
**Testimonial:** Famous or trusted person endorses something.

steps.title: WWI/WWII Posters
script: **Part 1: WWI/WWII Posters (5 min)** — Display 2–3 wartime posters. For each, ask:
“What do you notice first?” (Visual hook)
“What emotion does this create?” (Fear, pride, anger, guilt)
“Which propaganda technique(s) is this using?”
“Who was the intended audience? What action did they want?”

screen.question: What do you notice first? What emotion does this create? Which propaganda technique(s) is this using? Who was the intended audience? What action did they want?

steps.purpose: Read each wartime poster with the same four questions.

steps.title: Photo Manipulation
script: **Part 2: Photo Manipulation (4 min)** — Show examples: Soviet erasure of political enemies, Nazi manipulation of crowd sizes, Civil Rights–era photo cropping that changed meaning.
**Discussion:** *“Why is changing a photograph different from creating a poster? What makes doctored photos more dangerous?”*

screen.question: Why is changing a photograph different from creating a poster? What makes doctored photos more dangerous?

steps.purpose: Compare a poster everyone knows is made with a photograph people trust.

steps.title: Modern Connection
script: **Part 3: Modern Connection (3 min)** — Briefly show a modern example (political ad, manipulated social media image, deepfake concept). *“The techniques are identical — only the technology has changed. How can you apply what you’ve learned to images you see today?”*

screen.question: How can you apply what you’ve learned to images you see today?

steps.purpose: Bring the same techniques forward to images students see now.
students: The techniques are identical — only the technology has changed.

steps.title: From Awareness to Action
script: **Key takeaways:** Ask: Who made this? What do they want me to feel/do/believe? Identify the technique being used. Check: Is this fact, opinion, or manipulation? Seek multiple perspectives before forming opinions.
